# 1: Project Overview

This project aims to investigate how much a driver's individual technique influences race performance in Formula 1, rather than performance being determined by the machinery alone. By comparing Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri throughout the 2025 season, I hope to better understand these differences since both drivers compete for the same team and have access to similar machinery, resources, and team strategies. I will be examining telemetry data, particularly speed, throttle application and braking behaviour, alongside tyre compound and tyre age, to explore how driving techniques and tyre-related decisions affect race pace across straight, high-speed corners, and low-speed corners, where the data is available.

## 2.2.1: OpenF1

**Producer and authority.** OpenF1 is an open-source project maintained by nine contributors(br-g, adrielfrederick, keerth 1gowda, JesusGranizo, Ragha02, MukulS07, aksharbhagwandin, NiklEVer26 and FestinBiju). Its mission is to make Formula 1 data accessible to everyone.It is an unofficial data service, it is not an official FIA or Formula 1 provider.

**Original Dataset Purpose.** The purpose of the original dataset during the race is for teams to use timing and telemetry information to monitor car performance, driver behaviour and race strategy and after the race the teams can analyse that information to understand what happened and inform decisions for future races. 

**Collection method.** The original data comes from sensors installed in the cars and from race timing and tracking systems.However, the exact process OpenF1 uses to obtain and process all of its data has not been fully verified.

**Coverage and resolution.** The scope of my research focuses on the 2025 formula 1 season, specifically Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri across 24 races. In  the data source, I was looking for variables such as speed, throttle application, tyre age, tyre compound, braking, lap times, and car location, and I found records containing these variables. The data source has lap data recorded per lap, tyre information per stint, and telemetry data recorded multiple times per second. For my data audit, I examined one track, the Bahrain Grand Prix, to investigate the available variables. I also checked whether records were available for both drivers across all 24 tracks, which they were. I just, however did not fully verify the completeness and accuracy of every variable across the entire season. 

**Licence.** The OpenF1 GitHub repository contains a licence called Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 4.0 International Licence. The licence allows noncommercial sharing and adaptation of the material it covers.Users must give appropriate credit and follow ShareAlike requirements when sharing adaptations. It is unclear whether this licence covers the original Formula 1 telemetry data, so redistribution rights are still not clarified. 


**Access.** I found OpenF1 while searching for Formula 1 data online.I retrieved it on on 9/11/26.After investigating three possible sources, I selected OpenF1 because I encountered problems accessing the other data source FastF1. I then checked whether OpenF1 contained the variables needed for my research. With the help of AI, I retrieved the data directly from OpenF1 API into R using jsonlite::fromJSON() function (which we learnt in class after I had use AI). I was able to access historical data without creating an account or paying a fee because I was using 2025 data and from 2023 the data was free. The only problem I encountered was HTTP 429 errors when making multiple request,to see if the data I needed was available, which temporarily limited my access to the data. 

**Known problems.** While testing OpenF1, I noticed some limitations in the data. One 2025 race session returned only one lap record for Oscar Piastri, so I would need to determine whether this was due to an early retirement or missing data. I also noticed unusual telemetry values, where throttle and braking measurements reached 104, even though throttle is generally measured on a 0–100 scale and braking is represented using binary values. Another limitation is that OpenF1 provides car location data but does not directly identify whether each measurement was recorded on a straight, high-speed corner, or low-speed corner.


```{r source-1-load}
# getting the raw lap data from the 2025 Bahrain Grand Prix
library(jsonlite)
library(dplyr)

#filters through to OpenF1, find the content with laps and the session key to find a particular race. 
raw_1 <- jsonlite::fromJSON("https://api.openf1.org/v1/laps?session_key=10014")

#shows the structure of the raw data
dplyr::glimpse(raw_1)

#displays the first 6 rows
head(raw_1,6)
```

The output contains 1129 observations and 16 variables from the 2025 Bahrain Grand Prix. Some of the variables include lap number, lap duration, driver number, sector timing, etc. This information will help me filter the data to find the 2 driver numbers I am studying and compare how long it took them to finish a lap and a sector, etc 


## 2.3: Investigated and rejected sources

Jolipca-F1: I discovered it through F1DataStop, the same website where I found the other data providers,I rejected it because I first audited OpenF1 and it had everything I needed so I didn't see the point.
FastF1: I tried to investigate it, because its README on GitHub seemed very convincing but when I tried to retrieve data it was giving me so many errors and so i moved on with OpenF1.

## 2.4: What I could not find

OpenF1 did not directly provide classifications for different sections of the circuit, such as straight, high-speed, and low-speed corners. However, when I plotted the location data for the Bahrain Grand Prix, I was able to identify the general shape of the circuit and observe changes in speed. Although I could visually identify corners, I could not yet distinguish between the high-speed and low-speed corners. I do not currently see this as a reason to change my research question, but if I cannot reliably classify the corners, I may narrow my research question and generalize some of the detailed variables.

# 4: Consent and identifiability


**Consent.** I did not collect the data myself, as it was already available through OpenF1. The data describes the performance of Formula 1 drivers during official races, and I am using it for academic research. From what I found, the collection and use of telemetry data are governed by contracts and the Formula 1 regulations rather than separate consent from drivers but I can't say for sure what the exact agreements are and if the cover the public sharing of this data in particular.

**Identifiability.** My research focuses on 1 team (McLaren), and its 2 drivers (Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri). The smallest group is one diver. Both are identifiable and their racing performance data is publicly available.

**How sensitive data will be used.** The data I am using is about the drivers' racing performance and doesn't include private or sensitive information. I will keep their names and drivers numbers because they are important for my comparison but i won't publish the raw telemetry data un till I confirm that I have permission to do so.

# 5: Exclusions and harms

## 5.1: Excluded data from the audit

I did not permanently remove any data, I just filtered the dataset to Bahrain, that was after I made sure all 24 races where there ,then I filtered again to check for Lando and Piastri and looked through that filtered data set to see if I have the things I needed but that was just testing to see if i had the important things I have not decided which or if I will be excluding any data for my final analysis. Using only Bahrain for my auditing can affect my analysis but i don't know for sure if all variables found in Bahrain was recorded for the rest so there could be a possibility that my data source could be useless because I solely based choosing the data on the fact it had the variables for 1 race.

## 5.2: Who could be harmed

This could negatively affect the drivers in question since my research isn't considering every single detail and is taking out weird laps so people could ignore that the research doesn't account for every little things and could be misused by fans or the media to make one driver look worse than the other

## 5.3: Unreleased working data

I will not publish the raw telemetry data because I am still unsure if I have the permission to redistribute it but i plan on sharing my R code.
